 3 Australian Dividend Stocks With Yield Over 3%
 November 8, 2026, 02:21 UTC BA Bailey Pemberton Rising mentions of inflation on corporate earnings calls are a reminder that payouts you can see and touch matter more than ever. Reliable Australian dividend stocks paying more than 3% can help turn that pressure into regular cash flow while you watch rate and price headlines move around. This article walks through three income ideas from our high yield shortlist and explains what makes their dividends look more resilient.
 The three stocks highlighted here offer a compelling starting point if you want exposure to higher yielding businesses with well covered, growing and stable dividends. However, if you want the pick of this theme, these 5 dividend aristocrats stocks are the best of the best.
 Advertisement Computershare (ASX:CPU)
 Overview: Computershare runs share registries, corporate actions and employee share plans worldwide, generating recurring fee income that helps support regular dividends.
 Operations: The group earns most revenue from Issuer Services of about US$1.3b and Corporate Trust of about US$1.0b across primarily US and UK-linked markets.
 Market Cap: A$24.9b
 For the Dividend Powerhouses theme, Computershare matters because its registry and transfer agency work generates relatively steady cash flows that can support ongoing payouts, while interest income and capital markets activity vary in the background.
 "Margin income declined by 5.4% during the half, although Computershare subsequently increased its FY26 margin-income guidance to approximately US$740 million due to higher-than-expected client balances." 
 What ultimately happens to those client balances and the fees associated with them could influence future payout strength and consistency.
 That payout story starts with those client balances, and the full narrative for Computershare shows how margin income, capital cycles and risks could be quietly reshaping Computershare's dividend engine.
 ASX:CPU Earnings & Revenue Growth as at Nov 2026 BHP Group (ASX:BHP)
 Overview: BHP Group is a global resources giant that produces iron ore, copper and coal, using its Pilbara iron ore cash flows to support substantial dividends.
 Operations: BHP generates about US$29.0b from copper, US$23.9b from iron ore and US$5.6b from coal, with China its largest customer market.
 Market Cap: A$292.9b
 BHP Group gives this dividend screen heavy exposure to iron ore driven cash generation, backed by a broad mix of other commodities that help support ongoing payouts.
 "A strong pipeline of copper and potash projects positions BHP Group to benefit from a global surge in decarbonization efforts and electrification initiatives, with rising demand for critical minerals expected to influence future revenues." 
 What happens if just one pressure point on future copper and potash execution shifts could be crucial for dividend strength and valuation expectations.
 That pressure point is exactly where the full narrative for BHP Group shows how BHP Group's decarbonization projects, capital discipline and payout profile could be quietly decoupling from short term commodity swings.
 ASX:BHP Earnings & Revenue Growth as at Nov 2026 Commonwealth Bank of Australia (ASX:CBA)
 Overview: Commonwealth Bank of Australia is a major retail and business lender, using its home loan and deposit franchises to generate income from interest and banking fees.
 Operations: The group earns A$13.4b from Retail Banking Services and A$9.7b from Business Banking, with additional contributions from New Zealand and institutional activities.
 Market Cap: A$280.0b
 Commonwealth Bank of Australia matters for this Dividend Powerhouses screen because its large mortgage and deposit base can generate recurring income that helps support sizeable payouts from a diversified banking platform.
 "Growing competitive intensity in digital payments and deposit products, as fintechs and digital-first rivals target Commonwealth Bank of Australia’s core profit pools, could pressure net interest margins and fee income if deposit pricing and transaction fees are forced lower." 
 The real test for future income investors is whether one slowly building cost and risk pressure ultimately bites into those rich banking margins.
 That margin question is exactly where the full narrative for Commonwealth Bank of Australia shows whether Commonwealth Bank of Australia’s profit engine is quietly accelerating or whether rising digital costs are starting to bite.

 DA DanielOliveira on Airbnb · 2 days ago Today's Q3 answers the question this update left open, whether the Q2 acceleration would last. Nights and Seats Booked grew 16%, up from the 10% you cite for Q2, and Gross Booking Value grew 21% to $27.7B. Revenue was $4.9B, up 19% (16% excluding currency), against about $4.75B consensus, and first-time bookers grew 13% against your 11%. The full-year adjusted EBITDA margin target moves to about 36% from at least 35.5%. Two caveats: the Q4 guide of $3.22B to $3.28B includes about 2 points of currency help, and management says it is "closely monitoring ongoing developments in EMEA".  1 | 0 DA DanielOliveira on Atlassian · 2 days ago Today's Q1 FY27 guide updates two inputs here. Subscription ARR growth for FY27 is now about 18.5%, a touch above the 18% cited, but total revenue growth is guided at about 13.75%, below the 14.9% this valuation assumes, though both were raised tonight from August's 18% and 13%. The shape matters more than the level: Q1 grew 24% to $1,772M, the Q2 guide of $1,825M to $1,835M is about 15%, and on FY26 revenue of $6,572M the full-year guide leaves roughly 9% growth for the second half (my arithmetic). Data Center revenue is guided down about 16% for the year, and the normalizing migration benefit you flag shows in the cloud guide: about 26% for FY27 after 31% in Q1.
